::: {.hidden}
$$
\newcommand{\expr}[3]{\begin{array}{c}
#1 \\
\bbox[lightblue,5px]{#2}
\end{array} ⊢ #3}
\newcommand{\ct}[1]{\bbox[font-size: 0.8em]{\mathsf{#1}}}
\newcommand{\abbr}[1]{\bbox[transform: scale(0.95)]{\mathtt{#1}}}
\def\True{\ct{T}}
\def\False{\ct{F}}
$$
:::

#### The model

Let's say a bit more about the model, $\mathcal{M}_{\textit{Eng.}}$.

(@ex-english-model-definition) $\mathcal{M}_{\textit{Eng.}} = ⟨D_{\textit{Eng.}}, \{\True, \False\}, I_{\textit{Eng.}}⟩$

The domain, $D_{\textit{Eng.}}$, we can take to be the set $\{\ct{j}, \ct{b}\}$:

$$D_{\textit{Eng.}} = \{\ct{j}, \ct{b}\}$$

Let's also say a thing or two about the interpretation function, $I_{\textit{Eng.}}$.
Consistent with our grammatical rules, we will:

- interpret noun phrases as elements of the domain,
- interpret verb phrases as sets,
- interpret connectives as functions from pairs of sets to new sets.

Here we go:

(@ex-english-interp)
	$I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{Jo}) = \ct{j}$ <br>
	$I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{Bo}) = \ct{b}$ <br>
	$I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{runs}) = \{\ct{j}, \ct{b}\}$ <br>
	$I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{jumps}) = \{\ct{j}\}$ <br>
	$I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{and}) = g \text{   (where }g(s_{1}, s_{2}) = s_{1} ∩ s_{2}\text{)}$

Alright.
It is time to apply our lexicon definition and grammatical rules from earlier---together with this model definition---to an example expression of English.

#### Deriving an example

Here's a derivation of the expression $\textit{Jo jumps and runs}$.
(Note that you may need to scroll right to see everything.)

\begin{prooftree}
\AxiomC{$⟨\textit{Jo}, I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{Jo})⟩ ⊢ np$}
\AxiomC{$⟨\textit{jumps}, I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{jumps})⟩ ⊢ vp$}
\AxiomC{$⟨\textit{and}, I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{and})⟩ ⊢ con$}
\AxiomC{$⟨\textit{runs}, I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{runs})⟩ ⊢ vp$}
\RightLabel{Rule 2}\TrinaryInfC{$⟨\textit{jumps and runs}, I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{and})(I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{jumps}), I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{runs}))⟩ ⊢ vp$}
\RightLabel{Rule 1}\BinaryInfC{$⟨\textit{Jo jumps and runs}, I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{Jo}) ∈ I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{and})(I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{jumps}), I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{runs}))⟩ ⊢ s$}
\end{prooftree}

#### Simplifying the result

Taking $g$ to be the function providing the meaning of *and* in (@ex-english-interp), we can simplify the meaning derived above as follows:

$$I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{Jo}) ∈ I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{and})(I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{jumps}), I_{\textit{Eng.}}(\textit{runs}))$$
$$= \ct{j} ∈ g(\{\ct{j}\}, \{\ct{j}, \ct{b}\})$$
$$= \ct{j} ∈ \{\ct{j}\} ∩ \{\ct{j}, \ct{b}\}$$
$$= \ct{j} ∈ \{\ct{j}\}$$
$$= \True$$

#### Final thoughts

It is worth going back up to the model definition and inspecting the meanings we provided for *jumps* and *runs*.
Hopefully, you can convince yourself that *Jo jumps and runs* really [should]{.underline} be true.
I think it is then worth reflecting on the fact that we actually got this intuitive result in the end, simply by applying the rules of our grammar---carefully, but ultimately in a completely deterministic and mindless way---and then simplifying the resulting metalanguage expression.
